section.title: Israel Chosen and Idols Exposed
section.sectionRationale: This chapter continues the Book of Comfort's sustained argument against idolatry, moving from tender assurance that God will pour out His Spirit on Israel's descendants to one of Scripture's most vivid satires of idol-making, a craftsman using half a log for fuel and half to carve a god, before closing with the LORD's own joyful announcement that He has redeemed Jacob and blotted out its sin like a vanishing cloud.
section.thesis: The LORD who formed Israel from the womb and will pour out His Spirit on its descendants alone deserves worship, for no idol, carved by the same hands that use its other half for cooking fire, can see, know, save, or even recognize its own foolishness, while the LORD blots out sin and calls His people to return to Him.
section.frameNote: Six movements: the LORD's tender assurance and promised outpouring of the Spirit; His declaration as the first and the last, the only Rock; the folly of idol makers exposed; the extended satire of the blacksmith and the woodworker; the idol worshiper's blinded, deluded heart; and the closing call to remember and return, since the LORD has already redeemed Jacob.

units.label: Do not fear, O Jacob My servant

verses.text: But now listen, O Jacob My servant, Israel, whom I have chosen.
This is the word of the LORD, your Maker, who formed you from the womb and who will help you: “Do not be afraid, O Jacob My servant, Jeshurun, whom I have chosen.
For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and currents on the dry ground. I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants, and My blessing on your offspring.
They will sprout among the grass like willows by flowing streams.
One will say, ‘I belong to the LORD,’ another will call himself by the name of Jacob, and still another will write on his hand, ‘The LORD's,’ and will take the name of Israel.”

units.label: I am the first and the last

verses.text: Thus says the LORD, the King and Redeemer of Israel, the LORD of Hosts: “I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me.
Who then is like Me? Let him say so! Let him declare his case before Me, since I established an ancient people. Let him foretell the things to come, and what is to take place.
Do not tremble or fear. Have I not told you and declared it long ago? You are My witnesses! Is there any God but Me? There is no other {{tsur|Rock}}; I know not one.”
All makers of idols are nothing, and the things they treasure are worthless. Their witnesses fail to see or comprehend, so they are put to shame.
Who fashions a god or casts an idol which profits him nothing?
Behold, all his companions will be put to shame, for the craftsmen themselves are only human. Let them all assemble and take their stand; they will all be brought to terror and shame.

units.label: The blacksmith and the woodworker
units.note: half for the fire, half for a god

verses.text: The blacksmith takes a tool and labors over the coals; he fashions an idol with hammers and forges it with his strong arms. Yet he grows hungry and loses his strength; he fails to drink water and grows faint.

The woodworker extends a measuring line; he marks it out with a stylus; he shapes it with chisels and outlines it with a compass. He fashions it in the likeness of man, like man in all his glory, that it may dwell in a shrine.
He cuts down cedars or retrieves a cypress or oak. He lets it grow strong among the trees of the forest. He plants a laurel, and the rain makes it grow.
It serves as fuel for man. He takes some of it to warm himself, and he kindles a fire and bakes his bread; he even fashions it into a god and worships it; he makes an idol and bows down to it.
He burns half of it in the fire, and he roasts meat on that half. He eats the roast and is satisfied. Indeed, he warms himself and says, “Ah! I am warm; I see the fire.”
From the rest he makes a god, his graven image. He bows down to it and worships; he prays to it and says, “Save me, for you are my god.”

units.label: Blinded eyes, deluded hearts
units.note: is this not a lie in my hand

verses.text: They do not comprehend or discern, for He has shut their eyes so they cannot see and closed their minds so they cannot understand.

And no one considers in his heart, no one has the knowledge or insight to say, “I burned half of it in the fire, and I baked bread on its coals; I roasted meat and I ate. Shall I make something detestable with the rest of it? Shall I bow down to a block of wood?”
He feeds on ashes. His {{sakal|deluded}} heart has led him astray, and he cannot deliver himself or say, “Is not this thing in my right hand a lie?”

units.label: Return to Me, I have redeemed you
units.note: sins blotted out like a cloud

verses.text: Remember these things, O Jacob, for you are My servant, O Israel. I have made you, and you are My servant; O Israel, I will never forget you.
I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Return to Me, for I have redeemed you.

Sing for joy, O heavens, for the LORD has done this; shout aloud, O depths of the earth. Break forth in song, O mountains, you forests and all your trees. For the LORD has redeemed Jacob, and revealed His glory in Israel.

tsur.gloss: Rock, a title for God emphasizing His unshakeable stability, permanence, and reliability as a foundation and refuge. Isaiah's declaration that there is no other Rock deliberately contrasts the LORD's solid, self-existent reality with idols carved from ordinary wood, a foundation no craftsman shaped and no fire can consume.

sakal.gloss: Used here in a form describing being deluded, led astray, or foolish, the opposite of true wisdom and discernment. The idol worshiper's sakal, deluded, heart cannot even ask the one obvious question, is this thing in my hand a lie, showing that idolatry does not merely lack wisdom but actively blinds the mind against it.

basic.context: This chapter moves from the LORD's tender promise to pour out His Spirit on Israel's descendants to one of the Bible's most pointed satires against idol worship: a craftsman uses half a log to warm himself and cook his dinner and the other half to carve a god he then bows down to and begs for salvation. The chapter closes with pure celebration, since the LORD has already blotted out Jacob's sin like a cloud that simply vanishes.
basic.hermeneutics: The idol-making satire is not exaggeration for its own sake; it exposes the built-in self-contradiction of idolatry, that the very hands shaping a supposed god are stronger and more real than the object they create. The chapter's central theological claim, that the LORD alone is the first and the last, the only Rock, sets up the naming of Cyrus in the very next section as proof that only the true God can declare the future before it happens.
basic.originalLanguages: The LORD declares there is no other {{tsur}}, Rock, a title emphasizing unshakeable permanence, in stark contrast to an idol carved from the same tree trunk used for firewood. The idol worshiper's heart is {{sakal}}, deluded or led astray, unable even to ask the plain question whether the object in his own hand might be a lie.
basic.typology: The promise to pour out the Spirit on Israel's descendants, verse 3, anticipates the fuller outpouring at Pentecost, Acts 2:17-18, when God's Spirit is given not merely to a nation but to all who call on the name of the Lord. The LORD's title, 'I am the first and I am the last,' verse 6, is claimed directly by the risen Christ, Revelation 1:17, 22:13.
basic.christ: The LORD's self-declaration, 'I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me,' verse 6, is precisely the title Jesus applies to Himself as the risen Lord, 'I am the First and the Last,' Revelation 1:17, and 'the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last,' Revelation 22:13, identifying Christ fully with the eternal, incomparable God of this chapter. The promise that sins are 'blotted out like a cloud,' verse 22, anticipates the complete forgiveness secured at the cross, where sin is not merely covered but truly removed.
basic.god: God is the eternal Rock, incomparable to any rival, who alone declared the future before it happened and alone deserves worship. He also delights to pour out His own Spirit and blessing on ordinary descendants and to blot out sin completely, calling His wandering people simply to return, since He has already redeemed them.
basic.crossReferences: Revelation 1:17 and 22:13 apply 'the First and the Last' directly to the risen Christ. Acts 2:17-18 records the fuller outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost anticipated in verse 3. Psalm 115:4-8 offers a similar satire of idols that cannot see, hear, or speak. Jeremiah 10:1-16 makes a parallel argument against the folly of idol worship.
basic.oneStory: This chapter's contrast between the powerless, self-made idol and the LORD who alone is Rock, Redeemer, and Spirit-giver runs through the whole of Scripture's insistence that salvation cannot be manufactured by human hands. It anticipates Christ, who claims the title 'the First and the Last' for Himself and completes the blotting out of sin this chapter only announces.

context.literary:
The chapter is a diptych, and its two panels are meant to be read against each other. The first half, verses 1 to 8, is a promise and a title; the second, verses 9 to 20, is a lampoon; and verses 21 to 23 return to promise and end in a hymn. The movement is a circle: the LORD who formed Jacob in verse 2 speaks again in verse 21, 'I have made you,' and between those two statements stand the people who form gods for themselves.

The key to the structure is one verb. The LORD is the one who 'formed you from the womb,' verse 2, and the idol makers in verse 9 are the 'formers' of images, from the same root. Who forms whom is the entire argument. In verse 2 the Maker forms a people and calls them by a name of endearment; in verses 9 to 17 people form a god and give it a name. The question the chapter is asking is which direction the forming runs.

The satire of verses 12 to 17 is carefully built. The blacksmith is described in a single verse, and he grows hungry and faint, verse 12. The woodworker gets four verses and an entire life cycle for the tree: planted, rained on, grown, felled, and then divided. The two uses of the tree are laid side by side in a way that makes the reader do the arithmetic. The same wood warms a man and cooks his meat and becomes his god, and the man at the end says 'Ah! I am warm; I see the fire,' verse 16, which is the only line of his own speech in the whole account, and it concerns the fire, not the idol. Verse 17 then gives the other thing he says, 'Save me, for you are my god,' and the story is complete.

Verses 18 to 20 move from the scene to the mind. The satire becomes a diagnosis, and the prophet asks why no one says the obvious thing. Verses 21 to 23 then turn the diagnosis around: the one who can see what the idol-maker cannot is invited to remember, return and sing.
context.historical:
The exiles lived inside the greatest idol culture of their day. Babylon's temples held cult statues that were made by skilled craftsmen, clothed, fed and carried in procession at festivals. The gods of a conquering people appeared to have won, and a captive population had a daily temptation to think so. The prophet's mockery would have been heard against the background of public processions in which a god was carried through the city, which Isaiah 46:1-2 describes as a burden on weary animals.

The practices behind the satire were real. Cult images were often made of wood overlaid with metal, and the workshop involved both the metalworker and the carpenter, as verses 12 and 13 describe. In some traditions a statue was ritually 'brought to life' by ceremonies that declared it no longer the work of human hands. The prophet's retort is that no ceremony can undo the fact that the god was made by the person who now prays to it. The detail 'like man in all his glory,' verse 13, may point to the human form that many images took, and to the fact that the god looks like its maker.

Jeshurun in verse 2 is a poetic name for Israel that appears at the end of Deuteronomy. The people who heard the book of Isaiah knew that Moses' song had said that Jeshurun grew fat and kicked and abandoned the God who made him, Deuteronomy 32:15. The prophet takes that name and gives it back in tenderness. The practice of writing on the hand, verse 5, may refer to tattooing or marking oneself with the LORD's name as a sign of belonging, and the verse is about people from outside, one who 'will take the name of Israel,' joining the covenant family.
context.canonical:
The satire of the idol maker belongs to a long line of Scripture's argument against idols. Isaiah has already sketched the metalworker and the carpenter in 40:18-20 and 41:6-7, and he will return to the burden of the gods in 46:5-7. The psalms pick up the same sneer, 'They have mouths, but cannot speak,' Psalm 115:4-8 and 135:15-18, and Jeremiah's version compares the idols to scarecrows in a melon patch, Jeremiah 10:3-5. Habakkuk asks what good an idol is when it is mute, Habakkuk 2:18-19. All of these agree with the psalmist's verdict that 'those who make them become like them,' Psalm 115:8.

The promise of the Spirit poured on a people sits within a larger run of such promises. Isaiah 32:15 expects a day when the Spirit is poured out from on high and the wilderness becomes a fertile field; Ezekiel promises clean water and a new heart, Ezekiel 36:25-27, and an outpouring of the Spirit on the house of Israel, Ezekiel 39:29; Joel looks to a day when the Spirit comes on all flesh, Joel 2:28-29. Peter says at Pentecost that Joel's prophecy is being fulfilled, Acts 2:16-18, and Paul says God poured out the Spirit on us richly through Jesus Christ, Titus 3:5-6.

The title 'the first and the last' belongs to a series, Isaiah 41:4 and 48:12, and returns on the lips of the risen Christ, Revelation 1:17, 2:8 and 22:13. The pairing of forgiveness and a call to return in verse 22 reaches into the New Testament's own call, 'Repent, then, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped out,' Acts 3:19. Paul's account of idolatry in Romans 1:21-25 is a long meditation on how people exchange the glory of the immortal God for images, which is the same exchange the satire exposes.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet is working on the imagination of his hearers. The temptation of the exile was not to reject the LORD in so many words but to be impressed by the visible and the successful, and arguments from doctrine would not have been enough. So he offers a scene in which the absurdity can be seen. A man plants a tree, rains grow it, he cuts it down, and he is warmed by one half and prays to the other. The hearers are meant to laugh, and then to stop laughing as they realise that something similar could be going on in their own hearts.

The intent is also pastoral. The chapter opens and closes with the word 'servant' and the promise that God has chosen and redeemed them. The mockery is not meant to humiliate Israel but to free it. The prophet wants the people to be so sure of who made them that no carved face in Babylon can claim their loyalty. The final summons, 'Return to Me, for I have redeemed you,' puts the redemption first and the return second, so that the people who are asked to turn back are told that the door is already open.

A second intention shows in the question of verse 7: 'Who then is like Me?' It prepares for the long argument about prophecy that reaches its peak in the naming of Cyrus. The chapter wants the hearers to start looking for the one voice that spoke before the event.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The prophet describes the way idols are made, and no one in Israel is commanded to carve one. What the passage does prescribe is the stance that follows from it: do not fear, remember, return, and sing. The directives of verses 8, 21 and 22 are addressed to the people of God and carry forward straightforwardly as calls to trust, memory and repentance.

The satire does not give believers a licence to mock the religious practices of neighbours. Isaiah is speaking to his own people, about the temptation that faces them, and with a purpose of restoring them, not insulting others. Paul in Athens shows a different tone, starting from the people's own poets and from an altar to an unknown god, Acts 17:22-29, though he reaches the same conclusion about images.

The statement that God has shut the eyes of the idol maker in verse 18 describes a judgment that comes through a kind of self-blinding, as Isaiah 6:9-10 also describes. It is not a doctrine that explains why any particular unbeliever does not believe, and it should not be used as a diagnosis of individuals. The passage itself places the blindness alongside the invitation to return.

debates.question: Is the idol-maker passage a fair picture of ancient idolatry, or is it a caricature?

views.label: A fair description from outside
views.case: The materials, the combination of metalwork and woodwork, and the daily practicalities are accurate to what a workshop would have involved. A person who made a statue from a tree that also supplied his fuel would have seen exactly this. The force of the passage comes from taking the process at face value.

views.label: A deliberate caricature
views.case: Ancient worshippers did not usually say they believed the statue was the god. They held that the deity was present in or through the image after rituals had been performed. On this view the prophet flattens the theology of his opponents to make the point, as satire does, and he does not claim to describe their official doctrine.

debates.bearing: The prophet is not setting out to give a fair account of rival theologies. He is making a claim about the nature of idolatry that holds even if the worshipper has a more refined belief: whatever you have made cannot be the one who made you. In that sense the satire holds at the level that matters, and it explains why the Bible's own writers use the same argument, Psalm 115:4-8 and Acts 17:29.

debates.question: What does 'He has shut their eyes,' verse 18, say about responsibility?

views.label: God hardens as judgment
views.case: The subject of the verb is God, and the verse stands in the line of Isaiah 6:9-10 and of Pharaoh's story. The people who persist in idolatry are given over to the blindness they have chosen, and God confirms them in it, as Paul describes in Romans 1:24 and 1:28.

views.label: The blindness is the natural result of the practice
views.case: Verse 20 says that his deluded heart has led him astray. The idol worshipper does not ask the obvious question because the thing he has built has trained him not to. Idolatry blinds by itself, and the text attributes it to God because He is sovereign over the outcomes of what people choose, as in Psalm 115:8.

debates.bearing: The text sets divine action and human fault side by side without choosing between them. The very next verse addresses the same people as God's servant and invites them to return. The blindness is real, and so is the invitation, and no one is told that the door has been closed.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for idol makers in verse 9 is yotserei fesel, 'formers of an image,' and the participle yotser is the same word used of God in verse 2, 'who formed you from the womb.' The same family describes the potter in 45:9. The chapter allows the same verb to describe both the Maker of a people and the makers of gods, so the reader has to ask who is forming whom.

Verse 9 also makes a pointed claim about the idol makers themselves: they are all tohu, which the BSB renders 'nothing.' Tohu is the word for the formless waste of Genesis 1:2, and Isaiah uses it for what the nations amount to before God, 40:17 and 40:23. Those who make gods of tohu become tohu. Isaiah 45:18 will say the LORD did not create the earth tohu, and 41:29 describes the idols themselves as wind and tohu. The word links the satire to the creation story: the idol maker takes the raw material of the Creator's world and returns it to formlessness.

'The things they treasure,' verse 9, translates a word from the root chamad, to desire or delight in. It is the verb of the tenth commandment, to covet, and of Eve's desire for the fruit in Genesis 3:6. The things that people delight in are the things that they are condemned for delighting in.

The title Jeshurun in verse 2 probably derives from yashar, upright, and the BSB footnote glosses it 'the upright one.' It is used elsewhere only in Deuteronomy 32:15, 33:5 and 33:26. In Moses' song, the name carries a rebuke, since Jeshurun grew fat and abandoned his Maker; here it is a term of affection. The prophet turns an old reproach into a new endearment.

Verse 3 pairs two pourings. The same Hebrew verb is used for pouring water on the thirsty land and pouring out the Spirit on the descendants, so that the Spirit is the water of a new fertility and the willows of verse 4 are the visible result. Verse 5 is a three-part description of belonging: one says 'I belong to the LORD,' another uses the name of Jacob, and another writes on his hand 'The LORD's.' The name of Israel is something that can be taken up by those who were not born to it.

Verse 20 says that the idol worshipper 'feeds on ashes,' ro'eh efer, and the verb ra'ah means to tend or graze as a shepherd. He is shepherding ashes. The same verb gives Cyrus his title in verse 28, 'My shepherd,' and Hosea says Ephraim 'feeds on the wind,' Hosea 12:1. The question the idol worshipper cannot ask is 'Is not this thing in my right hand a lie?', and the word is sheqer, falsehood.

Verse 21 says 'I will never forget you.' The Hebrew verb form is unusual, and some translations render it 'you will not be forgotten by Me,' which says much the same thing. Verse 22 puts the imperative after the perfect: 'Return to Me, for I have redeemed you.' The redemption is already done, and it is the reason for the command.

typology.type: Water and the Spirit poured out, verses 3 and 4
typology.fulfillment: The promise ties the Spirit to water, to thirst and to growth. Jesus invites the thirsty to come to Him and drink, saying that streams of living water will flow from within the one who believes, and John explains that this meant the Spirit, John 7:37-39. At Pentecost the outpouring Peter announces in Acts 2:17-18 reaches beyond a single nation, and Paul says the Spirit was poured out through Jesus Christ, Titus 3:5-6. The type is exceeded in that the Spirit now dwells in believers and not only rests on a people. It is still short of its full harvest, which is the willows by the stream grown into the tree of life, Revelation 22:1-2.

typology.type: The name written on the hand, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: Those who belong to God mark themselves with His name. The theme grows through Scripture: the LORD says He has inscribed Jerusalem on the palms of His hands, Isaiah 49:16, and the redeemed in Revelation have the Lamb's name and His Father's name written on their foreheads, Revelation 14:1. Paul says believers are sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, Ephesians 1:13. The correspondence moves from a mark that people place on themselves to a sealing that God does. The type is incomplete in that the hand-mark was a human act of devotion, while the seal of the Spirit is a divine act that guarantees what it marks.

typology.type: The carved image of man, verse 13
typology.fulfillment: The craftsman shapes the idol 'in the likeness of man, like man in all his glory.' It is a god made in the image of its maker. Scripture's answer is that humanity itself was made in the image of God, Genesis 1:27, and that the true image of the invisible God is not a statue but a person, the Son, Colossians 1:15. Where idols are mute and cannot save, the living image speaks and rescues. Paul tells the Athenians that since we are God's offspring we should not think the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, Acts 17:29. The type works as a contrast: it shows what the true image is by exposing the false.

typology.type: Sin blotted out like a cloud, verse 22
typology.fulfillment: The picture is of a morning mist that burns away until nothing is left of it. The promise is made before any sacrifice is described, as a statement of what God has done, and the New Testament shows how it was done. Christ bore sins in His body on the tree, 1 Peter 2:24, and Peter calls on his hearers to repent so that their sins may be wiped out, Acts 3:19. Colossians says God canceled the record of debt that stood against us, nailing it to the cross, Colossians 2:14. The correspondence is complete in effect, but the cloud image cannot show the cost, which is that the removal of the sin was carried out in the death of the Redeemer.

study.christ:
The surest link is the title in verse 6. The LORD calls Himself 'the first and the last,' and the risen Christ takes the same words to Himself. When John falls at His feet on Patmos, the figure lays a hand on him and says, 'Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last, the Living One. I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever,' Revelation 1:17-18. To the church at Smyrna He is 'the First and the Last, who died and came to life,' Revelation 2:8, and the book closes with the same title, Revelation 22:13. The title was used by the LORD to refuse any rival god, and it is given without apology to Jesus. A first-century Jew who read Isaiah 44:6 would hear it as a claim to be Israel's God. The addition 'who died and came to life' shows what Jesus does with it: the first and the last has entered death and come out.

The chapter's other two titles for the LORD, 'King' and 'Redeemer,' verse 6, find their meaning in the same person. The Gospels call Jesus the King of the Jews and show Him enthroned on a cross, and Paul says in Him we have redemption through His blood, Ephesians 1:7. Isaiah says the LORD has already redeemed Jacob, verses 22 and 23, and in Christ the cost of that redemption is made known.

The outpouring of the Spirit in verse 3 comes through Christ. Peter says of the risen and exalted Jesus that He has received the Spirit from the Father and has poured out what the crowd sees and hears, Acts 2:33. Jesus Himself speaks of the Spirit under the image of living water, John 7:37-39. So the water and the Spirit of Isaiah 44:3 meet in the one who invites the thirsty and then gives the Spirit.

The idol maker's cry 'Save me, for you are my god,' verse 17, has its reply in the story of a different prayer. A man who does not know what to pray says 'Lord, save me,' and the one who hears does so at once, Matthew 14:30-31. The salvation that the idol cannot give is given by the one who walks on water. The nations' idols could not save and the LORD declares there is no Savior besides Him; the New Testament says that a Savior has been born, Luke 2:11.

The promise of forgiveness in verse 22 is where the chapter reaches its greatest depth. The text announces it in the past tense, as though it were done, and the cross is where it was done. In Christ God was reconciling the world to Himself, not counting their sins against them, 2 Corinthians 5:19. The invitation to return fits Jesus' own call to repent and believe, Mark 1:15.

A caution is needed. The satire of idols is not a coded description of Christ, and the 'servant' of this chapter is Israel, verses 1, 2 and 21, not the Servant of the songs. The chapter points to Christ chiefly through its claims about who the LORD is, and the New Testament uses those claims directly.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is introduced by the way He relates to a people before He is described by what He is. He is the one who forms from the womb, verse 2, and who helps, and He addresses a nation whose ancestors had failed by a name of tenderness, Jeshurun. He chooses a people not because of their record but because He has made them His own. The word 'chosen' is used twice in the first two verses, and it comes before anything the people do.

He is the only one who knows the future. The challenge of verse 7, 'Let him foretell the things to come,' makes foreknowledge the credential of deity. The idols are silent about what is coming because they are silent about everything. The LORD says He has already told them: 'Have I not told you and declared it long ago?' verse 8. His knowledge is not a general capacity but a record of word and fulfilment, which the exiles can check.

He is also the one who knows nothing like Himself. 'There is no other Rock; I know not one,' verse 8. The statement is not only that there are no other gods but that He is not aware of any. Divine omniscience is brought to bear on the claim that rivals are not merely weak but nonexistent. The idols are not powerless gods but products of the workshop, and the LORD sees nothing to compare Himself with.

His love shows in how He speaks to the afraid. 'Do not tremble or fear,' verse 8, is the same word He has been saying throughout the book, and each time it rests on something He has done. The kindness of a God who says 'I will never forget you,' verse 21, is that He ties Himself to a people who are likely to forget Him. The image of a mother who cannot forget her child, Isaiah 49:15, stands near.

He is a God of grace before demand. Verse 22 gives the order: He blots out their transgressions, then He tells them to return, because He has redeemed them. Forgiveness is not the reward for coming back; it is what makes coming back possible. The chapter closes with the cosmos called to sing, the heavens, the depths of the earth, the mountains and the forest, because the LORD has acted. Creation is not just the stage but the choir, and it sings for a redemption that touches it too.

There is also a hard note. The God who gives sight also shuts eyes in judgment, verse 18, and the same God who holds a people tenderly also holds idol worshippers accountable. The chapter does not blur this. Yet the God who judges the idol maker invites him, in verse 22, to return, and so even the hardest word is spoken by one whose purpose is to save.

For worship, the chapter does two things at once. It asks us to examine what we have made and trust, and it gives us a reason to sing: the LORD has done it, and He has made us His own.

crossReferences.note: The LORD describes Himself as the one who calls the generations from the beginning, 'I, the LORD, am the first, and with the last I am He.' It is the earlier form of the title in 44:6 and shows that the claim to be first and last is the thread on which the whole argument against the idols is hung.

The prophet asks to whom God can be compared and then sketches the craftsman who casts an idol, overlays it with gold and finds a wood that will not rot. It is the first sketch of the scene that 44:12-17 paints in full colour, and it shows how the polemic is built up across the book.

The psalmist says the idols have mouths, eyes, ears and hands that cannot work, and that those who make them become like them. Isaiah 44:9-20 shows exactly how that happens, since the maker's own blindness mirrors the blindness of his idol.

Jeremiah describes a tree cut from the forest and shaped by a craftsman and decorated with silver and gold, and ends by contrasting such gods with the one who made the heavens. It is a close parallel to Isaiah 44 and shows that the satire was a shared part of the prophets' preaching.

Moses says Jeshurun grew fat and kicked, abandoning the God who made him and scorning the Rock of his salvation. Isaiah 44:2 uses the same name and 44:8 the same word for Rock, so the chapter answers Moses' song by promising that the God Jeshurun scorned has not scorned him.

Joel promises that the Spirit will be poured out on all flesh, on sons and daughters, old men and young, and even on servants. It widens the promise of Isaiah 44:3 and is the text Peter quotes at Pentecost, Acts 2:17-18, to explain what the crowd is seeing.

God promises to sprinkle clean water on His people, give them a new heart and put His Spirit in them. Water and Spirit are brought together here as in Isaiah 44:3, and the promise shows that the outpouring is for cleansing and for obedience as well as for blessing.

The LORD says He will never forget His people, as a mother cannot forget her nursing child, and that He has inscribed them on the palms of His hands. It sets His promise in 44:21 beside the mark that Israel writes on its own hand in 44:5, so that the people's sign of belonging is answered by God's.

The risen Christ lays His hand on the frightened John and says that He is the First and the Last, the Living One who was dead and is alive forever. It applies the title of Isaiah 44:6 to Jesus and joins it to His death and resurrection.

Peter calls his hearers to repent and turn back so that their sins may be wiped out. It matches the order of Isaiah 44:22, in which sins are blotted out and the people are called to return, and shows that the apostles heard the same invitation in the gospel.

Paul says people exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images and served the creature instead of the Creator. It gives the same diagnosis as Isaiah 44, that idolatry is a swap of the Maker for the made, and applies it to the whole human race.

study.oneStory:
The question under the chapter is the first question of Scripture: who is the Maker, and who is the made? Genesis answers that God forms humanity from the ground and breathes into it. The fall consists of reaching for something else, a fruit that promises to make us like God, and the story of idolatry is that same reach in a thousand forms. Isaiah 44 is the Bible's sharpest comedy about what happens when the made turns around and tries to make the Maker.

The chapter also shows how God's answer works. Before the satire He has already said 'I have chosen you' and 'I formed you,' and after it He says 'I have redeemed you.' The pattern of the whole Bible is there: creation, then the people's turn to what they can make, then a redemption that begins with God. The idol is the human attempt to secure what only the Creator can give, and the chapter says that salvation is not something that can be made.

Looking forward, the promise of Spirit and water points to Pentecost and to the sprouting of a people drawn from every nation, since the name of Israel is taken by those who were not born to it, verse 5. That broadens in the New Testament into a church that is a people for God's own possession, 1 Peter 2:9. The title that excludes rivals, 'the first and the last,' is taken by Christ, so that the Maker who formed Israel in the womb and the Redeemer who was dead and is alive are one.

The story ends with the idols gone. The last chapters of Revelation leave outside the city those who love and practise falsehood, Revelation 22:15, and there is no temple, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. The heavens that sing in verse 23 have their final song in the voices of every creature in heaven and on earth, Revelation 5:13, and the people who once carried their gods now bear one name, written where all can see, Revelation 22:4.

quiz.q: What does the LORD promise to pour out on Israel's descendants in verse 3?

options.text: His Spirit and His blessing.
options.note: Verse 3 states this promise directly, anticipating the later outpouring at Pentecost.

options.text: Military strength for conquest.
options.note: The promise given is the Spirit and blessing, not military might.

options.text: Wealth and material prosperity alone.
options.note: The specific promise is the Spirit and blessing, not merely material wealth.

options.text: A new set of written laws.
options.note: The promise concerns the Spirit and blessing poured out, not new legislation.

quiz.q: What title does the LORD claim exclusively for Himself in verses 6 to 8?

options.text: The first and the last, with no other Rock or God beside Him.
options.note: Verses 6 and 8 state this exclusive claim directly.

options.text: The greatest among many equally valid gods.
options.note: The opposite; the claim is exclusive, not merely superior among equals.

options.text: A god limited to ruling only over Israel's territory.
options.note: The claim made is universal and exclusive, not territorially limited.

options.text: A minor deity among a larger pantheon.
options.note: The claim made is total exclusivity as the only true God, not a minor role in a pantheon.

quiz.q: What absurd behavior does the extended satire of verses 12 to 17 describe?

options.text: A craftsman uses half a log to warm himself and cook food, and the other half to carve a god he worships and begs to save him.
options.note: Verses 15 to 17 describe exactly this self-contradictory behavior.

options.text: A craftsman carefully preserves an entire sacred tree without using any of it for ordinary purposes.
options.note: The opposite; the satire's point is that the very same wood is used for both fuel and the idol.

options.text: A craftsman refuses to use any wood at all for his idols.
options.note: The satire describes extensive wood use, both for the idol and ordinary fuel, not an avoidance of wood.

options.text: A craftsman sells his idols to foreign nations for profit.
options.note: The passage focuses on the craftsman's own worship of the object, not commercial sale to others.

quiz.q: Why can the idol worshiper not recognize his own folly, according to verses 18 to 20?

options.text: His eyes and mind have been shut so he cannot see, understand, or ask if what he holds is a lie.
options.note: These verses describe this spiritual blindness directly.

options.text: He has simply never seen an idol being made.
options.note: The text says he made the idol himself, using half the wood for cooking, so he witnessed the whole process.

options.text: He lacks access to any better religious teaching.
options.note: The passage attributes his blindness to a shut mind and deluded heart, not merely a lack of information.

options.text: He is secretly aware of the truth but chooses to lie to others.
options.note: The text describes genuine blindness and delusion, not conscious deception of others while secretly knowing the truth.

quiz.q: What has the LORD already done for Jacob according to verse 22?

options.text: Blotted out its transgressions like a cloud and its sins like a mist.
options.note: Verse 22 states this directly, describing complete removal of sin.

options.text: Permanently recorded its sins for future punishment.
options.note: The opposite; the image is of sins vanishing like a cloud, not being preserved for judgment.

options.text: Forgiven only a small portion of its sin.
options.note: The imagery of a cloud and mist vanishing conveys complete, not partial, removal.

options.text: Demanded further sacrifices before any forgiveness could occur.
options.note: The verse presents forgiveness as already accomplished, followed by a call to simply return, not further required sacrifice.

questions: The LORD promises to pour out His Spirit on ordinary descendants, not just leaders or priests. Where do you need to trust that God's Spirit is genuinely at work in your own ordinary life?

The idol maker uses half his wood for dinner and half for a god, without seeing the contradiction. What modern 'idols' do you use for both practical benefit and misplaced ultimate trust without noticing the contradiction?
The idol worshiper's heart was so deluded he could not even ask whether the thing in his hand was a lie. What belief or habit in your life might need that same honest question asked of it?

The LORD declares He has already blotted out Jacob's sin like a vanishing cloud, then simply calls the people to return. Is there a sin you are still trying to atone for yourself rather than simply returning to the God who has already forgiven it in Christ?

Jesus takes for Himself the title 'the First and the Last' claimed by the LORD in this chapter. How does recognizing Jesus's full identity with the eternal God change the weight you give His words and promises to you?

translationNotes.note: Jeshurun is a poetic, affectionate name for Israel, meaning roughly 'upright one,' used elsewhere only in Deuteronomy 32:15, 33:5, 26.
Writing the LORD's name on one's hand likely reflects an ancient practice of marking identity or ownership, here signifying deliberate, personal devotion to the LORD.
This extended satire against idol-making is one of the most detailed such passages in the Old Testament, paralleled in tone though not length by Psalm 115:4-8 and Jeremiah 10:1-16.
